articles.body: **Hello DEV 👋 I’m Shivani, and I’m Building My Way Into Tech Hey everyone! 👋** I’m Shivani, an engineering student who is slowly figuring out my way around the world of tech. I started with the basics of HTML and CSS, then moved into JavaScript, Git & GitHub, and eventually started exploring React, APIs, and backend development. And honestly, it hasn’t always been smooth. 😅 There have been plenty of: “Why is this code not working?” moments Git errors I didn’t understand Deployments that worked locally but broke online Projects that looked much better in my head 😂 But every broken project has taught me something. Recently, I’ve also been exploring open source, hackathons, DSA, and building projects instead of just watching tutorials.

articles.title: 664KB of expert answer keys, and an import graph is the only thing keeping them off your machine
articles.excerpt: CogniPrep's assessment centre section has 37 timed exercises: e-tray and in-tray inbox triage, written exercises, presentations, group discussions and role-plays. One is free to play in full, the rest…
articles.body: CogniPrep's assessment centre section has 37 timed exercises: e-tray and in-tray inbox triage, written exercises, presentations, group discussions and role-plays. One is free to play in full, the rest are behind a one-time unlock. You can see the list here: cogniprep.app/assessment-centre-practice Serialised, the library is 679,475 bytes . 37 scenarios, 280 items, 151 inbox messages, and attached to every one of those items the expert answer key and the written rationale explaining why each option is better or worse than the others. That number is the entire reason the module is split in two. The failure mode is a static chunk, not a prop The exercise runner is a client component. It has to be: timers, inbox state, draft answers, a review step. So the obvious thing happens.
articles.author: Daniel Pertu

articles.title: I don't want another AI assistant. I want my own on WhatsApp.
articles.excerpt: Every company seems to want to build my personal AI agent. Muse, Instinct, Dots. The demos are impressive. But I keep asking a different question: why should I need someone else's agent to answer a qu…
articles.body: Every company seems to want to build my personal AI agent. Muse , Instinct, Dots . The demos are impressive. But I keep asking a different question: why should I need someone else's agent to answer a question about my calendar? I wanted to text “What’s on my calendar today?” on WhatsApp and get an answer from my own setup. No new app. No hosted chatbot service holding the memory of my conversations. That idea stayed on my list because building it meant doing everything around the agent first: WhatsApp webhooks, message handling, memory, model calls, tools. A bot that says hello is easy. One that can look something up, remember what you meant, and reply usefully is another project entirely. So I built Wappy and made it free and open source. It is not another finished personal assistant.
articles.author: chetan sandeep renu

articles.title: Your migrated workflow rules still run. That is not the same as still working
articles.excerpt: Your migrated workflow rules still run. That is not the same as still working Key takeaways Missing data leaves a hole you can see. Broken logic leaves a rule that is present, enabled and wrong — ther…
articles.body: Your migrated workflow rules still run. That is not the same as still working Key takeaways Missing data leaves a hole you can see. Broken logic leaves a rule that is present, enabled and wrong — there is nothing to notice. Measured: a JSU condition of priority > 5 persisted on Cloud as priority = 5, because the target rule only accepted = and !=. The comparator was silently demoted. DC's REST API does not return workflow rule bodies. /rest/api/2/workflow gives summaries; workflowDesigner gives rule COUNTS. You can count the rules without being able to read them. Run order is not cosmetic: filters, then workflows, then app rules inside those workflows, then automation last — automation depends on the fields and workflows already existing. Verify by behaviour, not by presence.
articles.author: Mihai Perdum

articles.title: The Developer Triangle: DSA, AI, and the Skill That Actually Gets You Hired (as a Beginner)
articles.excerpt: If you're just starting out as a developer, you've probably noticed that everyone's advice contradicts everyone else's. One person swears you have to grind 500 LeetCode problems or you'll never get hi…
articles.body: If you're just starting out as a developer, you've probably noticed that everyone's advice contradicts everyone else's. One person swears you have to grind 500 LeetCode problems or you'll never get hired. Another says DSA is dead and you should just learn to use AI tools. A third says forget both, just build projects. And you're sitting there with a limited number of hours in your week, no idea who's right, so you either freeze — or you default to grinding DSA, because that's the loudest voice in the room. Here's the honest truth: they're all half-right. And the thing nobody's actually telling you is how the pieces fit together . So let me draw you the map I wish someone had drawn for me.

articles.body: There is something uniquely unsettling about empty video game spaces. Blown wide open in the wake of Backrooms , the concept of liminal horror has seeped out from internet forums and chat rooms to become a subculture all its own. But while a photorealistic house filled with blood and corpses has its own macabre dread, there’s something even more unsettling about PS1-era graphics, where blocky textures and eerie lighting can make even a mundane street corner feel steeped in Lovecraftian horror.
